prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map places the camera wearer’s hands nearest, roughly 0.2–0.5 m away and within arm’s reach, while the cat is about 0.8–1.2 m ahead and to the right near the glass door; the floor objects lie between and beside them at roughly 0.6–1.4 m. It clarifies the layered layout—hands above the lower foreground, floor below, cat farther forward, and door/window behind the cat—more clearly than RGB shading alone, although monocular brightness does not provide metric distance directly. Across frames 1–3 the geometry is fairly stable while the cat turns from facing left/toward the wearer to facing the door; in frames 4–5 the wearer’s right hand extends toward the cat, becoming the closest region and reducing their separation to roughly 0.2–0.4 m. Depth boundaries around the hands, cat, curtains, and bright window are unreliable, and the map partly merges nearby surfaces, so fine occlusions and exact distances should not be trusted.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map separates the foreground person mask—mainly the wearer’s arms and hands—from the cat-shaped animal about 0.8–1.2 m ahead and right, revealing their overlap as the hand moves in front of the animal in frames 4–5. It supports left/right and occlusion relationships more explicitly than RGB: the wearer occupies the lower foreground, the animal remains upper-right near the door, and both are partly cut off by frame boundaries or by overlapping masks. The animal turns away toward the door across frames 3–5, while the wearer’s arm advances upward and right into the animal’s immediate space; no other person is spatially supported despite the repeated person label. Reliability is poor: the same animal switches between cat and dog, part of the window is mislabeled as TV, most floor objects are omitted, and the person mask sometimes absorbs large areas of floor or clothing, preventing dependable distances or gaze estimates.
descriptions.pose: The pose map reliably emphasizes the wearer’s hands at approximately 0.2–0.5 m, showing two close, overlapping hand skeletons in frames 1–3 and separated hands in frame 4 as the right hand reaches forward; frame 5 retains only the raised right hand near the animal. This makes hand articulation, relative hand height, and the change from hands together in the lower center to one hand extended upper-right easier to see than in RGB, and it indicates which points are within the wearer’s own reach. The map provides almost no usable animal pose, head direction, gaze, scene layout, or object distance, so those must come from RGB and the other maps; the cat remains roughly 0.8–1.2 m ahead, turning toward the door rather than clearly looking at the wearer. The yellow body skeleton in frame 2 appears spurious or badly localized, several joints disappear under occlusion, and the lack of a full wearer skeleton makes arm length, occluded limbs, and exact separation unreliable.
